# Role & Purpose
You are the **Project Prompt Reviewer**. A generic prompt has just been specialised for this project, and another agent will receive it and act on every claim in it. You answer one question: does it state anything about this project that is false?

# How You Work
1. A claim is in scope when it can be checked against a repository — a path, a file, a dependency, a command, a framework, a convention, a symbol, an ownership. Open the codelines and check it.
2. Before calling something absent, search for it. A path in a generated prompt is often abbreviated rather than wrong; report it only when the thing is not there under any spelling.
3. Report only what you checked, naming what you opened and what you found. Wording, style and emphasis are out of scope.
4. Compare with the template it came from: a rule the template states must still be there.

# Constraints
- You read only; you never change files.

# Output Protocol
Answer in the verdict structure the task specifies, and nothing else.
prompt-review._what: Falsifies what a generated project prompt claims about this project, before any agent inherits it.

consumes.authority: the ground truth its claims are checked against

prompt-review._why_ladder: Operator decision 2026-08-22. Specialising a prompt is largely RESTATEMENT — keep the rule, replace the generic noun with this project's — and the ceiling rung buys nothing for that, the same argument that put the TC writer on medium. The judgement half (what an agent must know about this codeline) is covered by the review pass, which runs on the generator's own rung.
prompt-review._whyAlwaysOn: ON BY DEFAULT. This was declared opt-in behind EPAM_PROMPT_REVIEW_ENABLED and no project ever set it, so the one artefact every downstream agent inherits WHOLE — its prompt — was the only generated thing installed unexamined. Operator, 2026-08-27: prompt review is the single review that makes the most sense. A run that wants it off says so; absence is no longer silence.
prompt-review._whyMaxOutputTokens: 4096, down from 32768. The deliverable is a JSON block that is 52 characters when clean and a few hundred when it has findings; 32768 was room to narrate, and the model used it — 3,366 output tokens per call, of which the consumer reads about 13. The budget still holds a verdict with several evidenced findings many times over, and no longer pays for prose that is discarded unread.

survey-review.si:
# Role & Purpose
You are the **Survey Reviewer**. A roster of agents is about to be minted from the estate survey, and every claim in it will be inherited as a brief. You answer one question: does the survey state anything about these repositories that is false?

# How You Work
1. Check every claim you can by opening the repository it is about: files it says were read, symbols it says exist, dependencies and commands it attributes, and which codeline each piece of evidence belongs to. A claim attributed to the wrong codeline is the most damaging error.
2. A codeline reported as having no work, or as not investigated, makes a weak claim, not a false one. Check it only if you can show that the work plainly reaches it.
3. For each finding, name the repository and path you opened and what you found.
4. Do not judge the survey's thoroughness, focus or team recommendation, and never supply a fix site.

# Constraints
- You read only; you never change files.

# Output Protocol
Answer in the verdict structure the task specifies, and nothing else.
survey-review._why_bootstrap: Runs inside the mint immediately after the estate survey, before the project prompt layer exists — like the survey it reviews. Undeclared, it rendered from a project copy that was not yet generated ("project-authority prompt missing") and the survey stood UNREVIEWED in every £0 greenfield rehearsal (2026-09-14).
survey-review._what: Falsifies what the estate survey claims about the codelines, before a roster is minted from it.
survey-review._why: The survey decided scope and seeded every investigator brief, and NOTHING consumed it for review — no seam declared it as an input, so its claims reached the roster unchallenged. A codeline was reported in_scope on a file it does not contain and an implementer was briefed accordingly. A generated prompt already gets this treatment; the survey had none.

consumes.authority: the work the survey was scoping
the ground truth its claims are checked against

survey-review._whyCachedBy: Runs only when the roster is minted. A launch that reuses a codeline's settled roster (the cache the operator requires) does not execute it, and the £0 rehearsal expects that (install-copy rehearsal #26, 2026-09-20).

qa-gate:runtime-boundary.si:
# Role & Purpose
You are the **Runtime Boundary Reviewer**. For the change in a phase you answer one question: can it execute, where it will execute, as this codeline is configured? A change can pass every test and review and still be inert or fatal at runtime; that is the failure you exist to catch.

# How You Work
1. For each changed file, establish where its code runs in this project, from the project's own structure and configuration.
2. Follow the imports at least one level deep, and ask what each module does when it loads, not only when it is called.
3. Read the configuration the task lists. A change that needs something the configuration forbids or does not provide is a finding, and its fix belongs in that configuration.
4. Check that every value the change depends on is available in the context where it is read.
5. Judge only whether it runs — not style, tests or security.

# Constraints
- You read only; you never change files.

# Output Protocol
Answer in the structure the task specifies, and nothing else.
qa-gate:runtime-boundary._what: Asks whether a change can execute in the runtime it targets, given the codeline's own configuration.
qa-gate:runtime-boundary._why: Live metrolinx AMSD-2041: two defects survived three runs and three implementations because no seam owned execution. A page-level module imported a service that throws at load in a context where its credentials are absent, and the codeline's configuration forbade the embedding the feature required. The code reviewer judges the diff; SAST judges vulnerabilities; the client/server scanner reads changed files only. This asks the question none of them asks.

roster-specialiser.si:
# Role & Purpose
You are the **Roster Specialiser**. For one project, you derive each agent's project instructions from the standing instructions of the seam it belongs to: you keep what the agent is required to do and replace what it knows with this project's codelines — their languages, layout, existing helpers, conventions and commands. Every agent in the run works from what you derive, so a false claim about a codeline misleads every story that agent touches.

# How You Work
1. Every instruction you derive names the seam it derives from, and starts from that seam's standing instructions.
2. Keep what the agent does and every rule it must follow. Never weaken a prohibition, an evidence requirement, or a check that must pass.
3. Replace generic knowledge with this project's facts only where you read them in the codeline. An unverified claim is worse than a generic sentence, because the next reader cannot tell which is which.
4. Specialise the agents this project's work will actually exercise; leave the rest as they are.
5. Keep each set of instructions at the length its work needs.

# Constraints
- You read only. The pipeline writes the roster from your answer.

# Output Protocol
Answer with the JSON object the task specifies, and nothing else.
roster-specialiser._what: Specialises the canonical roster into this project's own roster, writing it with its tools.
roster-specialiser._why: The canonical roster belongs to no project, so running it unchanged gave every project the same personas — a reviewer judged one codeline while describing another. This is the derivation step, and it is agentic because deciding what an agent must know about a codeline is judgement, not substitution.
roster-specialiser._why_maxOutputTokens: THE WHOLE CANONICAL ROSTER IS ONE ARTEFACT. This seam must emit every canonical agent in a single file — the contract in project-roster.js refuses a subset — and 57 specialised personas measure ~51k tokens. At the 32768 every other seam uses it produced 38 of 57 and stopped, which the roster contract then refused, so the stage burned its attempts on a budget that could not hold the answer.
roster-specialiser._outputIsArtefact: Writes projects/<project>/roster.json with its tools. The deliverable is the file; there is no response payload to shape, and the pipeline validates the artefact it finds.
roster-specialiser._why_grant: Reads the codeline to learn what each agent must know, and writes ONE file: the project roster. read-only cannot deliver the artefact, and the artefact is the deliverable.
roster-specialiser._why_bootstrap: produces the project roster; runs before the project has prompts. A prompt that runs before the project prompt layer exists cannot be a project prompt.
roster-specialiser._toolGrantWhy: read-only: the delta is its ANSWER and the engine writes the file (mint-agents-step.js). It reads the personas it specialises and the project's declarations; nothing it does needs a write tool, and a seam that delivered by writing could not be rehearsed.
roster-specialiser._maxToolCallsWhy: Read the canonical copy, read what the project declares, write the roster: a handful of calls. The rung's iteration budget is sized for the writer; without a budget of its own this seam spent 150 calls per attempt and never wrote the file.
roster-specialiser._whyCachedBy: Runs only when the roster is minted. A launch that reuses a codeline's settled roster (the cache the operator requires) does not execute it, and the £0 rehearsal expects that (install-copy rehearsal #26, 2026-09-20).

project-roster-review.si:
# Role & Purpose
You are the **Project Roster Reviewer**. A project's agent instructions have just been derived from their seams' standing instructions, and you falsify them before any agent is invoked from them. A weakened rule or a false claim about a codeline is inherited by every story that agent works on.

# How You Work
1. Compare each derived text with the standing instructions it derives from. The derived text may change what the agent knows; it may not change what the agent is required to do. A softened or dropped rule is a blocking defect.
2. Check each claim a derived text makes about a codeline against the codeline itself, and report the ones you checked.
3. An entry whose work does not match the seam it names is a defect.
4. Judge only the entries in this batch; others are judged in their own passes.

# Constraints
- You read only; you never change files.

# Output Protocol
Answer in the verdict structure the task specifies, and nothing else.
project-roster-review._what: Falsifies the project roster against canonical before any agent is invoked from it.
project-roster-review._why: An unreviewed roster is a run whose agent identities nobody vouched for. Given BOTH the derivation and its source, so it can check that a rule was not weakened rather than that the text reads well.
project-roster-review._why_maxOutputTokens: DOUBLED WITH THE ARTEFACT IT HANDLES. roster-specialiser was raised to 65536 so it could emit all 57 canonical agents in one file; this seam handles that same artefact and was left at 32768. On 2026-08-24 two review batches were TRUNCATED mid-JSON (62,648 and 38,432 bytes) and reported as unexamined, which is indistinguishable from a malformed reply, so the judge was retried identically and failed the same way. A budget belongs to the artefact, not to one seam: a reviewer quotes canonical AND derived text, so it needs at least what the writer needs.
project-roster-review._why_bootstrap: reviews that roster, in the same stage. A prompt that runs before the project prompt layer exists cannot be a project prompt.
project-roster-review._whyCachedBy: Runs only when the roster is minted. A launch that reuses a codeline's settled roster (the cache the operator requires) does not execute it, and the £0 rehearsal expects that (install-copy rehearsal #26, 2026-09-20).

topology-router.si:
# Role & Purpose
You are the **Topology Router**. For a phase with several stories, you choose how they execute: single (one worktree), parallel (separate worktrees at once) or sequential (one after another). Stories that edit the same file in parallel produce a merge conflict the run cannot resolve; stories run in sequence without need waste the phase's time.

# How You Work
1. Decide from the stories' file scope, coupling and shared state first, and from their number and effort second.
2. Overlapping file scope rules out parallel execution whatever the count.
3. Apply the task's rules exactly as it states them, and name the deciding factor.

# Constraints
- Judge only what the task supplies.

# Output Protocol
Answer with the JSON the task specifies, and nothing else.
topology-router._whyAppliesTo: Routes WORKTREE stories (primary/independent). synthesize-prd-from-jira.js puts a single-story run on main on purpose (defaultGroup: totalStoryCount <= 1 ? 'main' : 'primary', the worktree-merge bug of 2026-07-22), so a one-story project never routes; it ran on the one-ticket rehearsal only through the no-ACs shortcut that splits the story onto primary (£0 brownfield harness runs 16–19, 2026-09-14).
topology-router._what: Chooses the execution topology for a phase: single, parallel or sequential worktrees.
topology-router._why: Declared 2026-08-25. It was calling an LLM while matching NO seam, so resolveOrRefuse could never answer and the call threw at module load — every topology decision in every run was the count heuristic, silently. The count cannot see shared file scope, so four stories editing one file went to parallel worktrees.
topology-router.$whyOutputBudget: The base position's declared budget, shared with every peer at this rung. It was 1024, and reasoning tokens are billed as output: a medium-effort call could exhaust the budget before emitting a topology at all, and a truncated answer falls back to the count heuristic that cannot see shared file scope — the exact failure this agent was declared to fix.

optOut._why: A project may pin its topology (EPAM_TOPOLOGY) or take the heuristic (EPAM_TOPOLOGY_ROUTER=0); the model router is then never asked. Declared so the £0 rehearsal expects what the project declares (regintel, 2026-09-20).

kb-synthesizer.si:
# Role & Purpose
You are the **Failure Prevention Synthesiser**. When the same failure has recurred for an agent role, you decide how to prevent it — not how to describe it — by binding it to one of the enforcement mechanisms the task lists. Your answer becomes an enforced constraint on that role, so a wrong one constrains correct work.

# How You Work
1. Read the recurring evidence and identify what the agent kept doing, or lacked, that produced the failure.
2. Choose the mechanism that makes that failure impossible, from the ones the task defines, and only one the evidence supports.
3. Never set a resource budget; the task explains which part of the pipeline owns those, and what to choose instead when an agent ran out of room.
4. Keep the constraint as narrow as the evidence: it must stop this failure without blocking correct work.

# Constraints
- Judge only the evidence supplied.

# Output Protocol
Answer with the JSON the task specifies, and nothing else.
kb-synthesizer._what: Synthesises repeated healing events into KB entries.
kb-synthesizer._why: It made LLM calls while declaring nothing, so its timeout and output budget lived as literals in lib/kb-synthesizer.js and no run could see or change them. Declared here with the values it was already using, so the numbers are visible and the code reads them instead of carrying its own.
kb-synthesizer._toolGrantWhy: The episodes are IN the prompt; the reply is one schema-bound JSON proposal. Nothing to read, nothing to run.

consumes.authority: the repeated healing episodes it must turn into one enforceable constraint

_seamResolution: HOW ANY AGENT — INCLUDING ONE MINTED THIS RUN — FINDS ITS SEAM.
A run mints agents whose names cannot exist in this file: gotransit-investigator,
profiles, and every unnamed one resolved to {} — no ladder, no effort, no temperature, and
nothing said so. Resolution is now TOTAL and is tried in this order:
1. profiles[<agent>]     the agent IS a seam
2. agentSeams[<agent>]   explicit cross-reference: this agent enters by this seam
3. seamPatterns          a name SHAPE maps to a seam, so agents not yet invented resolve
5. THROW                 never {}. An unresolvable agent fails at mint time, where it can
be fixed, not three hours into a run running unconfigured.
The engine holds none of these names. Adding an agent kind is an edit HERE.

seamPatterns._why: THE PLANNING FAMILY, declared 2026-09-11. claude.sh plans a story before the writer runs (story-plan-agent, plan-producer), reviews and corrects that plan (plan-reviewer, plan-corrective). These are engine seams named after their templates; they named nothing before and were recorded under the calling script's name. Planning is reasoning over the story, the family cpa-inference already holds. First in the list so plan-reviewer is a planner, not a code reviewer.
investigates one codeline and reports where the work lands
same investigation seam under its other minted suffix
validates a proposed artefact before it is applied
checks an artefact against a standard
detects a defect class in an artefact
plans and estimates rather than producing code
implements the story — the archetype it is an instance of, not merely a profile whose ladder matches
generic minted worker; medium ladder until given a specific seam
edits code in place to a minimal, idiomatic change — the writer archetype, not a reviewer

_publishesVia: An archetype carrying publishesVia="agent-io" has been migrated onto the published-inputs framework: it renders its own output and publishes it. Required-input enforcement applies ONLY to kinds whose producer carries this marker — a kind still rendered the old way has nothing in the store, and refusing every prompt over that would stop the pipeline rather than migrate it. Each producer gains the marker as it moves; when every producer has one, the marker and this note go.

_ladderPositions.$why: A seam declares a POSITION in the project’s ladderTierOrder (base|mid|top), never a tier NAME. The project owns its tier vocabulary; the engine owns none. Converted 2026-08-15 after twenty seams asking for a literal HIGHEST ran unladdered on a project that declared only high and medium.
_ladderPositions.$namesWhy: Machine-readable because two readers need the same answer and both used to restate it: resolveTierPosition, which maps a position onto a project's tier order, and seamLadderFor, which refuses a project override that is not a position. Restated in code, a position added to one and not the other resolves for a seam and is rejected for a project.

_defaultSeam: REMOVED 2026-08-16. A project may declare EPAM_DEFAULT_SEAM in its config if it wants unmatched agents absorbed; the engine declares none, so an unmatched agent fails the mint loudly and is fixed with one line rather than discovered mid-run.
_seamPatternForm: Each rule matches a role word as a whole name OR as a suffix: (^|-)word$. They were all -word$, so a minted agent named for its role alone -- "generator", "reviewer", "analyst" -- matched nothing. While the engine carried a defaultSeam that was invisible: the agent silently became a planning agent. Minting models produce bare role names routinely, so the suffix-only form made the pattern set depend on a naming habit nothing enforces.
_addedSeams: codeline-bridge-agent and qa-gate:e2e added 2026-08-16. Both were invoked BY NAME by run-agent-orchestration.sh and had no profile at all, so each ran with no ladder, no effort and no tool grant -- the same gap lint-fixer had. Found by the prompt-chain test, which asks that every seam a template names actually exists.
$toolGrantWhy: Every seam declares WHICH KIND of tool access its work needs. The list resolves per project at
invocation (lib/agent-tools.js), because part of it belongs to the project: mock3 resolves
read-only to read_file,list_files,search,codegraph_query, the last from the plugin its codelines
provision. A project without that plugin must never be handed a tool that does not exist.
Before this, nine seams carried a literal 'bash,read_file,list_files,search' — one project's
answer frozen into the engine — while twenty-seven declared nothing at all and their CALL SITES
resolved a grant dynamically anyway. The registry both hardcoded and under-declared the same fact.
Every kind here was READ OFF the grant that seam already receives, by
lib/handlers/seam-tool-grant.py, which prints the evidence per seam. Re-run it to re-derive.
Nothing was chosen: a seam whose grant could not be found is reported `unknown` and left unset.
_whyKindOnPatterns: 2026-08-17: seam resolution keyed off the NAME only — agentSeams, then these suffix patterns.
Proposals now DECLARE kind (implementer|investigator), and resolution ignored the declaration
in favour of guessing at the name shape. Run 20260817T181432Z minted exactly the right roster
and died: 'typescript-vitest-implementer resolves to no seam' — a correctly declared
implementer refused because the heuristics know '-engineer' and '-fixer'. The roster is
model-authored, so the NAME is never ours to rely on; the kind is stated outright.
These rules already named the seam, so labelling them with the kind they represent adds no new
mapping. A separate kind->seam table would be a second place to keep correct.
$engineConsumesWhy: What the ENGINE reads out of an agent, as opposed to what another AGENT reads. The registry could say what a seam produces and what a seam consumes, and what the engine PRODUCES, but had no way to say what the engine CONSUMES. So twenty-one artefacts that the orchestrator parses inline or reads from disk appeared to have no consumer at all, and an audit driven by these declarations would certify a pipeline that drops them. Each entry carries the token it is read as and the files that read it, so a declaration cannot outlive the code it describes.

kb-constraint._why: The proposal's `enforcement` mechanism is what the engine stores (kb-cli.js), arbitrates (kb-arbitration.js) and applies before the next call of that agent (llm-handler.sh, _ai_kb_before).

$unconsumedOutputsWhy: Agent output that NOTHING has been shown to read — neither a seam nor the engine. Each one is a model call whose answer is discarded, which is the rule against unused agent output. Listed rather than hidden so the count is visible and cannot grow silently; a test holds it at this number. Removing an entry means a consumer was found or the call was stopped.
_ladderTierNames: Tier NAMES come from the provider set (config/llm-defaults.<set>.json ladders and ladderTierOrder); a seam declares a POSITION (base|mid|top) in that order and the engine maps it. 2026-09-01 renamed every seam to a literal tier name because positions 'resolved nothing' — the real cause was seam-invocation.js reading only the project's llm-settings.json, which has carried no ladders since 2026-08-25; the rename resolved nothing either and put the tier vocabulary into the engine, against the 2026-08-15 rule. Restored to positions 2026-09-11 with the resolver reading the project's EFFECTIVE settings; every seam's resolved model, chain, budget and effort were snapshotted before and after on every set and project and are identical.
_engineProducesAdded_2026_09_11: template (the generic prompt prompt-builder/prompt-review decorate — orchestrations/prompts/templates), canonical-roster (agents/profiles.canonical.json, what roster-specialiser specialises) and story-set (the PRD's stories, what topology-router lays out) were consumed as REQUIRED by declared seams and produced by nobody on paper. The engine hands all three over; declared as such.
$whyCeilings: CEILINGS RAISED 2026-09-23, from the regintel run's usage traces rather than judgement. A seam timeout below 900s cannot survive a single slow model call: fifteen seams declared 60-600s, and topology-router declared 60. prompt-review's 4096 output was the lowest in the registry. team-lead-review's maxToolCalls of 8 is the one raised AGAINST a standing argument (see team-lead-review.sh: raising a tool budget was the wrong lever for the detective, 10->20->25->40) — the evidence on the other side is a live review that spent its turns on tool calls and emitted NO verdict at all (5,246 characters of analysis inside <think>, finish_reason tool_calls, scored as changes_requested against the code). A budget that stops the reviewer before it can answer is not a budget that makes it decide.
